title: An Appeal to the Gods at the Tower
type: A gathering at the Tower of Gael and petitions for a divine audience
dek: A difficult gathering at the Tower leads to prayers, departures and individual replies. Arjahn asks Heimr for answers, then asks how long grief lasts.

facts.Recorded span: 27–29, Month of Death · Year 3 of the Final War
facts.Gathering: Scribonia, Adelia, Elenia, Arjahn, Nymera, Olokun, Oya and Alyhotep
facts.What is established: The company petitions and disperses; Adelia repeats part of Nuru’s reply; Heimr speaks with Arjahn
facts.What remains open: A full divine assembly; complete answers about the Gate and history; the promised family reunion
facts.Later encounters: Nuru’s reply to Adelia; Heimr’s conversation with Arjahn; Fenwick’s departure for Prima

events: The Tower’s company petitions for a divine audience

body:
A request first discussed by the exhausted company in Babel brings old companions together at the Tower of Gael. Some want explanations, some want reassurance and some want to know why they were chosen. Before any answer comes, they have to get through a difficult conversation with one another.

Portals, embraces and an impatient request

Scribonia steps into the Tower of Gael through a portal with two companions, then calls for Adelia. He wants clerics to help petition the gods for a meeting. He has heard an account from Dumuzi and wants to compare it with what the gods themselves will say.

The room does not become solemn immediately. Oya runs toward Olokun with open arms, pushes past him and embraces Nymera instead. Olokun objects to his own sister rejecting his hug; Oya eventually gives him one and says she was joking. Nymera quietly checks whether Oya seems hurt, says she missed her and asks about the letter.

Scribonia calls Elenia away from her materials and brings Arjahn into the gathering. Adelia thanks him for being honest with her and offering guidance. He surprises her by initiating a hug, stays in the group embrace for a while, then steps back when it becomes too much.

Adelia says she has safeguards against interplanar travel and asks to be warned next time. When Arjahn assumes the Tower is her domain, she corrects him: she says she is strongest near Hope and weaker where they are sitting. She proposes moving closer to the tree. The surviving sequence does not show that move before the petitions begin.

Different reasons to ask, and a friendship under strain

Scribonia wants an account of history, the selection of arrivals through the Gate and the state of the war. He says he does not believe Dumuzi and wants to give the gods an opportunity to answer. A representative would do; he is not asking them to abandon their work for an immediate appearance.

Elenia thinks some questions have already been answered and dislikes asking busy gods to repeat themselves. She is sarcastic about Scribonia giving them the benefit of the doubt. He is hurt by the contempt he hears in her response and asks what he has done to deserve it.

She explains that the gods are individuals and that asking them collectively to account for one another’s actions is unfair. Scribonia answers that the company’s leaders also bear responsibility for one another. She later accuses him of trying to make himself a judge of the divine; he rejects that description. The argument ends without either accepting the other’s account of his motives.

Arjahn has his own reason for wanting their words. He says he has fought and died for the gods and will continue to fight, but needs to know whether the work matters. The mist still troubles him: even after the rescue, he struggles against the wish to run back toward the daughter he believed he saw. When Elenia asks whether he has tried asking, he answers, “This is me trying.”

Olokun supports the request while saying the discussion will not change his decision to oppose Death. He then turns his attention back to Oya. The questions matter differently to the people in the room; the gathering does not produce a shared judgment on the gods or verify a new history of the world.

The prayers they actually make

Arjahn calls Talan by name, recalls an earlier conversation and asks for honesty in return for the honesty expected of him. He wants to know how the war stands and how the Gate works. He explicitly allows for a later answer. This appeal does not establish that he has renounced another divine relationship.

Nymera looks toward a wall and asks Cala why she was chosen. She says she is trying and asks whether Cala will speak with her. Oya offers a prayer for Namo’o to hear them, remembering the kindness she associates with him. Alyhotep prays too, says his own gods feel distant and offers to keep asking or help the others.

Adelia attempts to reach the Tower’s altar and calls on Nuru. Scribonia later sends his own requests to Cala and Nuru, asking for a meeting with either the gods or their representatives. Elenia says speaking with the gods is a gift she does not want to abuse; she also attempts an intervention before departure. At the end of those appeals, no appearance or answered audience has yet been recorded. The later replies come individually rather than as the assembly the company requested.

The distinction matters for what follows. The group has made the request that Scribonia proposed at Skylight Refuge. No formal divine assembly or agreed answers follow before the company leaves.

A way home, money for Oya and an unanswered tap

After his appeal, Arjahn says he cannot transport himself for a week and asks for help returning to Babel-Ashur. Elenia offers to take them, while Scribonia says he has spent his most powerful spells getting everyone together. Arjahn thanks Elenia and tells her that he still cares for her despite the frustration. Their disagreement has not made her cease to matter to him.

Olokun checks Oya’s uncovered hands, feet and movements. The scene shows no visible sign of what he fears, while the argument has left her shaking. He puts an arm around her, then later tells her to stay and help protect Gael because Babel remains dangerous. He trusts her with work at home; the exchange does not grant her an unrecorded office.

They still tease each other. Olokun trips her during a hug, and she tells Arjahn to annoy him with a supposed fear of blobfish. Arjahn does not know what the fish is, so she makes him a quick drawing. Nymera gives Oya money she says is not useful to her in Babel, embraces her and promises to keep trying to make the world better for her.

The company steps through a Gate. Alyhotep gathers his helpers and leaves Lois a note before following. Those departures do not yet show the company arriving at its intended destination. Fenwick’s separate return to the Tower and withdrawal to rest keep the refuge in use beyond the gathering; his own later departure is recorded below.

In the later narrator follow-up, after the group has dispersed, Arjahn feels a gentle but firm tap on his shoulder. Adelia hears wind, waves and gulls after her appeal, followed by requests for perception and religion checks. This first follow-up does not yet identify the caller or supply the requested checks. The continuation then follows Adelia’s response and Arjahn’s encounter separately.

The words Adelia chooses to repeat

The perception and religion checks follow Adelia’s appeal. She notices Nuru’s presence in the patience of the birds, the rhythm of the waves and the wind around the Tower. A voice addresses her in her mind. The answer is personal, rather than a speech to the assembled company.

Adelia first begins repeating what she hears. The narrator makes the distinction clear: the words were addressed to her individually, though she can choose to share them. She then keeps the beginning to herself and repeats the part about gaining wisdom through mistakes rather than simply receiving knowledge. Her voice carries that part of Nuru’s answer and the unfinished thought about being summoned to account for mistakes.

The company’s request has therefore received a response, but not everyone is given everything Adelia hears. Her choice to share some words and keep others matters to what the people around her can know. The scene does not become a public hearing or resolve every question asked at the altar.

Fenwick also leaves the Tower in this continuation. He gathers his homunculus and his simulacrum and uses Plane Shift to return to Prima. The spell records support that departure; they do not identify a particular landing place within Prima or complete the separate expedition he had discussed earlier.

The visitor who answers Arjahn

The tap on Arjahn’s shoulder leads to a different conversation after the gathering has dispersed. He closes his eyes and releases the breath he has been holding. Scribonia’s questions are complicated, he says, but he has some of his own: whether the gods have deliberately misled them, what relationship they had with Dumuzi, how the Gate works and whether their fighting is enough.

Arjahn knows the request takes time from the war. He still needs to ask. After what the mist made him experience, reassurance is no longer a matter of having another tactic to try. He needs help to continue doing what he has already promised to do.

Heimr answers instead of Talan. He rejects the idea of the gods as one body speaking with one mind and acknowledges omissions and half-truths in their account of the past. His reply is partial and personal. It does not provide the full history of Dumuzi or an operating explanation for the Gate.

Arjahn understands being overextended, but answers that mortal fighters are dying too. Information they lack could be as necessary as any other weapon. He is grateful for the chance to speak and will not press every question now; he thinks Scribonia should continue asking. Heimr’s response challenges a further assumption: perhaps the people being asked do not possess the complete certainty Arjahn expects of them. That possibility enters this conversation as Heimr’s account, not as a newly verified explanation of the world.

A home builder without a home

Arjahn’s answer makes his anger plain. He blames Dumuzi for what happened to his family and says he wants him to suffer. His demand for knowledge does not come from accepting Death’s offer. He wants a way to hurt the enemy who has already hurt him.

He also recognizes something he had not allowed for: Heimr may be speaking from uncertainty of his own. Arjahn apologizes for trying to turn that pain into a weapon, even while admitting that he still thinks it could be useful. He reads Death’s anger as the anger of someone who feels betrayed and hopes to provoke it into a mistake. That remains Arjahn’s proposed strategy and interpretation, not an accomplished victory or proof of Death’s motive.

The vow survives the apology. Arjahn says he will remain in the fight until he dies. Then his question changes. He asks how long grief and forgiveness take, and how many eternities must pass before he can accept life as it is.

Heimr offers no fixed term. Some never find it, he says, but the earth is still a home for everyone. He calls Arjahn a home builder without a home and promises that, when it is all over, he will get him to his family. The exchange ends with that promise. It does not show a reunion, completed forgiveness or an end to the war.

The Tower petition has produced more than silence: Adelia has repeated part of Nuru’s reply, and Arjahn has received an answer and a promise from Heimr. These individual encounters do not establish a full assembly, a shared account heard by every companion, or answers to every question Scribonia brought to the Tower.

evidence.summary: The public gathering and social actions are witnessed in RP. Adelia’s range, safeguards and proposed move remain her account and plan; no new map geometry, completed relocation or universal travel rule is inferred.

sections.title: Different reasons to ask, and a friendship under strain

evidence.label: RP scenes & narrator observations
evidence.summary: Competing motives, explanations and criticism remain attributed. Arjahn’s later account of the mist does not establish that his family was physically present. Protected cosmological explanations are excluded; the gathering does not adjudicate them.
